context_blurb:
Scientists learn about the world by measuring it, and you can too. A ruler, a thermometer or a timer turns words like long, hot and fast into numbers that anyone can check. But a number is only worth trusting when it comes from the right tool, read the right way.

Length is measured with a ruler, in centimetres and metres. Temperature is read from a thermometer, in degrees Celsius. Volume, the space something takes up, comes in litres and millilitres. Mass, the amount of matter in something, is found with a balance, in grams and kilograms. So a reading in kilograms, such as 6 kilograms for a big pumpkin, is always a mass.

A spring scale measures force, which is a push or a pull. Clip one to a brick and tug, and the spring inside stretches. The harder the pull, the farther the spring stretches, so the pointer shows how hard the brick is pulled. Force is counted in newtons, after Isaac Newton.

Liquids are measured in a graduated cylinder, a narrow glass tube marked in millilitres. Water clings to the glass and creeps up its sides, so the surface sags in the middle. Read the level at the bottom of that curve, with your eye level with it. Looking down from above lines the water up with the wrong mark.

Pour sand into a cup on a balance, and the reading is for the cup and the sand together. To find the mass of the sand alone, take away the mass of the empty cup. Setting the empty balance to zero first is no help, since the cup's mass still ends up in the reading.

Bacteria are living things too small for any eye to see on its own. A hand lens makes things look at most about 10 to 20 times bigger, not nearly enough. To see bacteria, a scientist needs a microscope, which makes things look from about 40 to hundreds of times bigger.

Science also needs fair tests. Say some students wonder whether a large parachute takes longer to float down than a small one. In a fair test, only one thing changes: here, the size. The load, the drop height and the timing all stay the same for both, so if one parachute takes longer to land, only the size can cause that difference. Change two things at once, and nobody can tell which one mattered.

Even a fair test needs more than one try. Drop a ball from the same height again and again, and the bounces will not all match. Each drop comes out a little different, because of small slips such as letting go a bit too high or reading the metre stick at a slant. So scientists repeat the very same trial and compare the results, or average them.

A bigger magnet is not always the stronger one: a small neodymium magnet can out-pull a much bigger magnet of a weaker kind. When careful, repeated tests go against a prediction, the honest move is to change your idea to fit the results, not the results to fit your idea. A test that proves an idea wrong has not failed; it has taught you something true.

Not every question suits a fair test. A fair test can answer whether bean plants grow taller in sun or in shade: grow some in each, keep everything else the same, and measure them. Counting the pebbles in a jar is useful, but nothing is changed and compared, so it is not a fair test. And no test can settle a matter of taste, like which song is prettiest, or what people ought to do.

Scientists record their numbers in tables and graphs. Picture temperatures read every hour from morning till evening. A line graph joins those readings with a line, so you can see at a glance how the temperature climbs and drops through the day. A bar graph compares separate groups instead, and a tally chart counts how often something happens.
